title: Portless
subtitle: How named .localhost URLs replace port numbers in local dev
throughline: one browser request to myapp.localhost — from a typed name, through the proxy, to a dev server on a random port, and back

chapters.title: Names, Not Port Numbers
chapters.blurb: How portless run turns a random dev-server port into a stable https://myapp.localhost URL.

steps.title: Names, Not Port Numbers
steps.spoken: Every dev server hands you a port number. Portless hands you a name instead.
steps.displayNarration: **portless** replaces `localhost:3000` with a stable, named URL like `https://myapp.localhost`. This chapter follows one launch.

steps.title: The port-number problem
steps.spoken: When you start a framework, it picks a port and prints something like localhost colon three thousand. Restart it and the number can change, so you end up memorizing ports instead of apps.
steps.displayNarration: A framework binds an ephemeral port and the **browser** must target it by number — `localhost:3000`. The number is unstable across restarts.

steps.title: Infer the name
steps.spoken: So you run portless run next dev. The first thing it does is infer a name for your app, from the package name, the git root, or the directory, and turn that into the host myapp dot localhost.
steps.displayNarration: `portless run next dev` calls `inferProjectName()` — package.json name, git root, then directory — and `sanitizeForHostname()` to derive the host `myapp.localhost`.

steps.title: Pick a free port
steps.spoken: Next it asks for a free port. findFreePort probes the four thousand to four thousand nine hundred range until it gets one that actually binds, skipping the ports browsers refuse to talk to.
steps.displayNarration: `findFreePort()` returns a bindable port in `4000-4999`, skipping `BLOCKED_PORTS` (the WHATWG bad-port list).

steps.title: Register the route
steps.spoken: With a name and a port in hand, it writes a route: the host myapp dot localhost maps to port four one two three, tagged with this process id. That mapping is the whole contract.
steps.displayNarration: `store.addRoute(hostname, port, process.pid)` records `{ hostname: "myapp.localhost", port: 4123, pid }` into `routes.json`.

steps.title: Spawn the app on that port
steps.spoken: Then it launches your actual command, next dev, with the PORT environment variable set to that port. Most frameworks read PORT and bind there without any code changes.
steps.displayNarration: `spawnCommand()` runs `next dev` with `PORT=4123`. Frameworks that ignore `PORT` (Vite, Astro, etc.) get `--port` auto-injected by `injectFrameworkFlags()`.

steps.title: Visit the name
steps.spoken: Now you open myapp dot localhost over https. The dot-localhost names resolve to your own machine automatically, so the request lands on the portless proxy listening on port four forty three.
steps.displayNarration: `.localhost` auto-resolves to `127.0.0.1`, so `https://myapp.localhost` reaches the **portless proxy** on port `443`.

steps.title: Look up and forward
steps.spoken: The proxy reads the host, looks it up in the route table, finds port four one two three, and forwards the request straight to your dev server. The reply streams back the same way.
steps.displayNarration: The proxy matches the Host against its routes and proxies to `127.0.0.1:4123`, piping the response back to the browser.

steps.title: One name, end to end
steps.spoken: That is the whole loop. One command found a port, registered a name, and started your app; one URL now carries the browser through the proxy to that app and back.
steps.displayNarration: **Recap:** `portless run` registers `myapp.localhost -> 4123`; the browser hits the proxy, which forwards to the app and streams the reply home.

chapters.title: The Proxy's Round Trip
chapters.blurb: Inside createProxyServer: how one request is matched by Host, guarded against loops, and proxied to the right app.

steps.title: The Proxy's Round Trip
steps.coverSubtitle: One request, from Host header to backend and back
steps.spoken: Every named URL flows through one small proxy. Let's follow a single request through it.
steps.displayNarration: `createProxyServer()` is built on Node's `http` module — no external deps. We trace one request through `handleRequest`.

steps.title: Read the host
steps.spoken: A request arrives. The first job is to learn who it is for, so the proxy reads the host. Over HTTP two that is the authority pseudo-header; over HTTP one point one it is the Host header. Then it strips any trailing port.
steps.displayNarration: `getRequestHost()` prefers the HTTP/2 `:authority` pseudo-header, falling back to `Host`. The port is dropped: `host.split(":")[0]`.

steps.title: Guard against loops
steps.spoken: Before doing anything, it checks a hop counter carried in a header. If a request has already passed through portless five times, it is almost certainly a forwarding loop, so the proxy stops it with a five-oh-eight and an explanation.
steps.displayNarration: The `x-portless-hops` header is read; at `MAX_PROXY_HOPS` (5) the proxy returns `508 Loop Detected` instead of forwarding. Each hop increments the counter.

steps.title: Ask for the routes
steps.spoken: Now it needs the route table. The proxy calls getRoutes, a callback that returns the current routes. Crucially this is an in-memory snapshot, so matching costs nothing on disk.
steps.displayNarration: `getRoutes()` is invoked per request and returns `cachedRoutes` — an in-memory list, not a disk read on the hot path.

steps.title: Match exact, then wildcard
steps.spoken: findRoute matches the host against that list. It tries an exact match first. If strict mode is off, it can also fall back to a wildcard: a sub-domain like tenant dot myapp dot localhost can resolve to the myapp route.
steps.displayNarration: `findRoute()` returns the exact `hostname` match first; when `strict` is false it falls back to `host.endsWith("." + r.hostname)` for wildcard subdomains.

steps.title: When nothing matches
steps.spoken: If no route matches, the request does not just fail silently. The proxy returns a four-oh-four page that actually lists the apps currently running, with the exact command to start the one you asked for.
steps.displayNarration: No match -> `404 Not Found` via `renderPage()`, listing active routes and the `portless <name> your-command` hint. (A loop returns `508`.)

steps.title: Forward to the backend
steps.spoken: On a match, the proxy rewrites the request for the backend. It adds the forwarded headers, the original protocol, host, and client address, restores the real Host so vhost-aware apps still see it, and opens an HTTP request to the loopback address on the matched port.
steps.displayNarration: `buildForwardedHeaders()` sets `x-forwarded-for/proto/host/port`; HTTP/2 pseudo-headers are stripped and `Host` restored, then `http.request({ hostname: "127.0.0.1", port: route.port })`.

steps.title: Stream the reply back
steps.spoken: The backend's response is piped straight back to the client. Because the front door may be HTTP two, the proxy strips the hop-by-hop headers that HTTP two forbids, like connection and transfer-encoding, before sending it on.
steps.displayNarration: `proxyRes.pipe(res)` streams the reply; for TLS clients the `HOP_BY_HOP_HEADERS` (connection, keep-alive, transfer-encoding, upgrade...) are deleted to stay HTTP/2-legal.

steps.title: The full round trip
steps.spoken: So one request is read, counted, matched, rewritten, forwarded, and streamed home, all inside a single dependency-free handler.
steps.displayNarration: **Recap:** read Host -> hop guard -> `getRoutes()` -> `findRoute` -> forward to `127.0.0.1:port` -> pipe the response back.

chapters.title: Trust on First Run
chapters.blurb: How portless serves real HTTPS with HTTP/2: a one-port byte-peek demux, a local CA, and per-host certificates via SNI.

steps.title: Trust on First Run
steps.coverSubtitle: Real HTTPS and HTTP/2, with no browser warnings
steps.spoken: Portless serves real https by default. To do that it has to become its own certificate authority.
steps.displayNarration: HTTPS with HTTP/2 is on by default. On first run portless generates a **local CA**, trusts it, and binds `443`.

steps.title: One port, two protocols
steps.spoken: Both encrypted and plain traffic can land on the same port. So the listener is a plain TCP server that peeks at just the first byte of each connection before deciding what it is.
steps.displayNarration: A wrapping `net.createServer` reads one byte (`socket.read(1)`) and `unshift`es it back, so TLS and plain HTTP can share a single listener.

steps.title: 0x16 means TLS
steps.spoken: That first byte is the tell. A value of hex sixteen is the start of a TLS handshake, so the connection is handed to the HTTP two secure server. Anything else is plain HTTP, handed to a tiny redirect server.
steps.displayNarration: `buf[0] === 0x16` (TLS ClientHello) -> the `http2.createSecureServer` (with `allowHTTP1`). Otherwise -> a plain `http` server that redirects.

steps.title: Bounce plain HTTP up
steps.spoken: If you arrive over plain HTTP, you do not get an error. The redirect server replies with a three-oh-two pointing at the same name over https, so links just upgrade themselves.
steps.displayNarration: The plain-HTTP path returns `302` to `https://<host>` (same port). There is also a standalone `createHttpRedirectServer` for port 80.

steps.title: Which certificate?
steps.spoken: For the TLS connections, the handshake needs a certificate that matches the exact name being requested. The secure server asks a server-name callback, handing it the host the browser wants.
steps.displayNarration: The HTTP/2 server is created with an `SNICallback`. During the handshake it receives the `servername` (e.g. `myapp.localhost`) and must return a matching `SecureContext`.

steps.title: Mint a per-host leaf
steps.spoken: On first run portless generates a local certificate authority, or CA, valid for ten years. Then, because the dot-localhost names cannot use a wildcard certificate, it signs a fresh leaf certificate for each exact host, caching it on disk and in memory.
steps.displayNarration: `ensureCerts()` creates the CA once; `createSNICallback` then mints a per-host leaf (RFC 2606: no wildcard at the `*.localhost` public-suffix boundary), cached on disk and in a `Map`.

steps.title: Tell the OS to trust it
steps.spoken: A self-signed CA only helps if the system believes it. So portless adds the CA to the operating system trust store: the login keychain on a Mac, the distro CA directory on Linux, the root store on Windows. After that, no browser warnings.
steps.displayNarration: `trustCA()` installs the CA into the system trust store — macOS `security add-trusted-cert`, Linux `update-ca-certificates/trust`, Windows `certutil` — then writes a trust marker.

steps.title: Green padlock, end to end
steps.spoken: Put together: one port peeks a byte to split TLS from plain, the secure server asks for a name, portless signs a trusted leaf for it, and the browser shows a clean, valid https connection.
steps.displayNarration: **Recap:** peek byte -> route TLS to the HTTP/2 server -> `SNICallback` -> CA-signed leaf -> trusted by the OS -> valid HTTPS.

chapters.title: The Shared Route Table
chapters.blurb: How RouteStore keeps routes.json safe across many processes with a lock, stale-PID cleanup, and a live-reloading proxy.

steps.title: The Shared Route Table
steps.coverSubtitle: One JSON file, many processes, zero corruption
steps.spoken: Every app and the proxy share one small file. Keeping it consistent is its own little problem.
steps.displayNarration: All routes live in one `routes.json` under `~/.portless`, written by every `portless run` and read by the proxy. `RouteStore` keeps it safe.

steps.title: Grab the lock first
steps.spoken: Many processes may register at once, so a write never happens unguarded. addRoute first acquires a lock by making a lock directory. A directory create is atomic, and a lock left behind by a dead process is reclaimed after a timeout.
steps.displayNarration: `addRoute()` calls `acquireLock()` — `fs.mkdirSync(routes.lock)` is atomic. A lock older than `STALE_LOCK_THRESHOLD_MS` is removed and retried with backoff.

steps.title: Write the entry
steps.spoken: Holding the lock, it loads the current routes, drops any old entry for the same host, appends the new host, port, and process id, writes the file, and releases the lock.
steps.displayNarration: Inside the lock: `loadRoutes()`, drop duplicates of `hostname`, push `{ hostname, port, pid }`, `saveRoutes()`, then `releaseLock()`.

steps.title: Self-healing entries
steps.spoken: Reads clean up after crashes. When routes are loaded, every entry is tested by signalling its owning process id with signal zero. If that process is gone, the entry is dropped, so stale routes never pile up.
steps.displayNarration: `loadRoutes()` keeps only entries where `isProcessAlive(pid)` (`process.kill(pid, 0)`) succeeds; dead-owner routes are filtered out and the cleaned list persisted under lock.

steps.title: Conflicts and --force
steps.spoken: What if the name is already taken by a live process? Then addRoute refuses, throwing a conflict error, unless you pass force, in which case it sends the old owner a termination signal and takes over the name.
steps.displayNarration: If a live process already owns `hostname`, `addRoute` throws `RouteConflictError` — unless `force`, which sends `SIGTERM` to the old PID and replaces the entry.

steps.title: The proxy watches
steps.spoken: The proxy never re-reads this file on every request. Instead it watches the file for changes. When a registration lands, the watcher fires.
steps.displayNarration: `startProxyServer` sets `fs.watch(routesPath, ...)`; if `fs.watch` is unavailable it falls back to polling. Changes are debounced.

steps.title: Reload into memory
steps.spoken: On a change, after a short debounce, it reloads the routes into an in-memory cache. That cache is exactly what getRoutes returns to the request handler, which is why matching stays cheap.
steps.displayNarration: `reloadRoutes()` refreshes `cachedRoutes = store.loadRoutes()`; the proxy's `getRoutes: () => cachedRoutes` serves matches from memory.

steps.title: Safe to share
steps.spoken: So the table is a single file: locked while written, self-healing on read, and mirrored into the proxy's memory the moment it changes.
steps.displayNarration: **Recap:** lock -> write `{host, port, pid}` -> dead-PID cleanup on load -> `fs.watch` -> debounced reload into `cachedRoutes`.

chapters.title: Zero-Config Startup
chapters.blurb: How the proxy auto-starts, reuses its last config, and fails loudly in CI — then the whole journey, end to end.

steps.title: Zero-Config Startup
steps.coverSubtitle: It just works after a reboot — and the whole picture
steps.spoken: You should never have to start the proxy by hand. Let's see how it brings itself up, then retrace the whole journey.
steps.displayNarration: The proxy auto-starts when you run an app, reusing the last run's settings. This chapter closes with the end-to-end recap.

steps.title: Is a proxy already up?
steps.spoken: When you run an app, portless first checks whether a proxy is already listening and answering on the expected port. If one is, there is nothing to start.
steps.displayNarration: `ensureProxyRunning()` calls `isProxyRunning(proxyPort, tls)` first; if the proxy already responds, it returns `{ started: false }`.

steps.title: Reuse the last config
steps.spoken: If it does need to start one, it does not silently fall back to defaults. It reads the previous run's port, TLS setting, and top-level domain from small marker files, so a restart or reboot keeps the same behaviour. Explicit environment variables still win.
steps.displayNarration: `readPersistedProxyState()` restores the last `port`, `tls`, and `tld` (from `proxy.port` / `proxy.tls` / `proxy.tld`). Explicit `PORTLESS_*` env vars override.

steps.title: Start it (and elevate)
steps.spoken: Then it spawns portless proxy start and waits for it to answer. Binding the privileged port four forty three needs elevation, so on a Mac or Linux it auto-elevates with sudo. But with no terminal, or in CI, it exits with a clear message instead of hanging on a prompt.
steps.displayNarration: It `spawnSync`s `proxy start`, then `waitForProxy`. Port `443 < PRIVILEGED_PORT_THRESHOLD` needs sudo; non-interactive (no TTY / `CI`) exits with guidance, not a prompt.

steps.title: Then your app
steps.spoken: With the proxy up, the app is launched with its assigned port and registered as a route, exactly as we saw at the start.
steps.displayNarration: Back in `runApp`: `findFreePort` -> `addRoute` -> `spawnCommand` with `PORT` set, so the dev server binds the assigned port.

steps.title: The name is live
steps.spoken: And now the name is simply live. You open myapp dot localhost and the proxy carries you to the app.
steps.displayNarration: `https://myapp.localhost` now resolves through the running proxy to the freshly registered app — no manual setup.

steps.title: The whole journey
steps.spoken: That is portless end to end. A name becomes a port, the proxy auto-starts and trusts itself, a request finds its route in memory, gets forwarded to your dev server, and the reply streams home, all under one clean URL.
steps.displayNarration: **Recap:** auto-start proxy -> register `myapp.localhost -> 4123` -> browser hits the proxy -> `findRoute` -> forward to the app -> stream the response back.
